analysis.one_liner: Makes buyout funds legally responsible for debts and harms at companies they take over, and limits profit extraction.
analysis.headline: The Stop Wall Street Looting Act was introduced on November 18, 2024, with 7 original sponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets the private equity business model. When a fund buys a company, the fund and its managers would become personally liable — jointly and severally — for the company's debts, pension obligations, and legal penalties, so they could no longer walk away from a failed takeover. The bill would bar a fund from paying itself big dividends, buybacks, or fees out of an acquired company for four years, make it easier to claw back asset-stripping in bankruptcy, put workers' unpaid wages and severance ahead of other creditors, crack down on executive bonuses in bankruptcy, and close tax loopholes used by fund managers and health care real estate trusts.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private investment funds — the bill's findings note nearly 12 million people work for such companies — would gain most directly: unpaid wages and severance would get higher priority in bankruptcy, executive bonuses would be limited, and funds could be held liable for job losses and pension harm. Consumers and employees at retailers like Sears and Toys "R" Us (cited in the bill's findings) would benefit from rules against loading companies with debt and stripping assets. Nursing home residents and patients would gain from a ban on Medicare/Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to real estate trusts. Retirement savers and pension funds would gain from new disclosure and fiduciary rules on the funds they invest in.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and communities where buyout-owned companies operate

how_it_helps.text: A fund that controls an acquired company, and anyone holding an active interest in it, would be jointly and severally liable for that company's debts, pension withdrawal liabilities, legal penalties, and worker-protection violations — and contracts indemnifying the fund against this liability would be void [S2].

For four years after a takeover, the acquired company could not pay large dividends, buybacks, redemptions, or similar distributions, and could not close a plant and move the work overseas; employees and creditors could sue to void violating transfers and recover attorney's fees [S2].

In bankruptcy, workers' wage and severance priority would rise to $20,000 per employee with no 180-day cutoff, severance and welfare-plan contributions would become priority claims, and penalties for labor-law violations would become administrative expenses paid ahead of unsecured creditors [S2].

Executive bonuses, retention payments, and exit compensation in bankruptcy would be tightly limited and must not be disproportionate to what the nonmanagement workforce received; bankrupt companies could not pay special executive compensation if they cut worker severance in the prior year [S2].
Court sales of a bankrupt company's assets would have to weigh which buyer best preserves jobs and employment terms, and buyers would be bound by their representations to the court [S2].

Federal health care programs would be barred from paying providers that sell their assets to, or pledge them as collateral to, a real estate investment trust — aimed at the common practice of nursing homes and hospitals leasing their buildings back from REITs [S2].

Fund managers would lose the carried-interest loophole: profits from managing investment partnerships would be taxed as ordinary income rather than at lower capital-gains rates, and partnership interests received for services would be valued at liquidation value [S2].

Private funds receiving government funds would have to disclose pay ratios, beneficial owners, and use of proceeds, and could not acquire companies or pay shareholder distributions for two years; the bill also imposes fiduciary duties, fee-and-return disclosures, risk-retention rules for securitized corporate debt, and protections for striking workers against permanent replacement [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, their managers, and their general partners would bear the largest costs: unlimited liability for portfolio-company debts, a surtax taking payments from acquired companies up to the full top tax rate, new limits on the interest deduction for over-leveraged portfolio companies, and ordinary-income treatment of carried interest. Health care real estate investment trusts would lose the Medicare/Medicaid revenue of provider tenants and a special tax rule. Private credit lenders and firms that securitize risky corporate debt would face disclosure and risk-retention requirements. Some costs could pass through to investors in these funds, including pension funds, in the form of lower or more cautious returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds, their managers, and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: Unlimited joint-and-several liability for everything a portfolio company owes — including acquisition debt and pension withdrawals — could make funds far less willing to buy struggling companies at all, which supporters would have to weigh against the goal of protecting those companies' workers [S2].

The surtax on payments from acquired companies, the stricter interest-deduction limits, and ordinary-income treatment of carried interest would raise the cost of the buyout model, and some of that cost would likely flow to the pension funds, endowments, and retirees who invest in private funds as limited partners (whom the bill deliberately excludes from liability) [S2].

The four-year ban on post-takeover distributions and the restriction on relocating operations overseas would limit the flexibility of owners to restructure, which defenders of the industry argue can be part of saving a failing business rather than looting it.

The bill is sweeping — touching bankruptcy law, the tax code, securities law, and Medicare/Medicaid payment policy at once — so its combined effects on capital availability and on companies' cost of borrowing would be difficult to predict precisely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to identifiable groups of people: workers owed wages when a buyout goes under, residents of nursing homes whose landlords are Wall Street-owned trusts, and gift card holders and consumers left holding claims against a bankrupt retailer (the bill raises the consumer deposit priority to $1,800). The costs fall on a well-defined, wealthy industry, with some possible pass-through to pension-fund returns — and the bill's drafters visibly tried to limit that pass-through by exempting passive limited partners and pension funds from the liability rules. The main honest uncertainty is whether liability this broad would chill rescues of genuinely failing companies along with the looting the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act on November 18, 2024, joined by six original cosponsors: Senators Baldwin, Brown, Sanders (I), Merkley, Smith, and Markey [S1][S2][S3].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S4].

That referral was the only action the bill ever received; the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S4].
Introduced six weeks before the end of a two-year Congress, with no Republican support and no committee scheduling, the bill had no realistic path to a vote [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds and their managers, health care real estate trusts, and private credit lenders are better off, because the existing rules that let them extract fees, dividends, and tax advantages from acquired companies remain in place unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and the funds' managers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 18, 2024 and assembled six original cosponsors

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, Brown, Sanders (I), Merkley, Smith, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; no other senators joined

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the six weeks before the Congress ended, leaving it without any committee action

sides.party_line_note: All seven original sponsors were Democrats plus one independent (Sanders); no Republican cosponsored, and with the bill dying in committee no votes were ever taken to test bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Private equity funds and their managers
industries.note: The bill strikes at the core of the buyout model: unlimited liability for portfolio-company debts and pensions, a four-year ban on big dividends and buybacks after a takeover, a surtax on payments extracted from acquired companies, and clawback of asset transfers. Fund managers profit from fees and distributions regardless of how the investment turns out, which is exactly what the bill's findings say it aims to end [S2].

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: Providers that sell their buildings to a REIT would lose all Medicare and Medicaid payments, and the tax rules that let REITs hold health care property through taxable subsidiaries and shelter REIT dividends would be repealed. The bill's stated concern is that nursing homes and hospitals end up paying rent to extractive landlords while care suffers [S2].

industries.industry: Hedge funds and investment managers (carried interest)
industries.note: Profits from managing investment partnerships would be taxed as ordinary income instead of at capital-gains rates, closing the carried-interest loophole for managers of buyout, real estate, and other investment funds [S2].

industries.industry: Private credit lenders and securitizers of corporate debt
industries.note: The bill would require greater visibility into non-bank direct lending and private credit, and impose risk-retention rules so lenders and securitizers of risky corporate debt keep some of the risk they currently pass to investors [S2].

industries.industry: Pension funds and other institutional investors in private funds
industries.note: Pension funds are deliberately excluded from the new liability rules, but new fee, return, and fiduciary-disclosure requirements could expose them to information they have avoided, while higher costs on fund managers could trim the returns pensions expect from private equity [S2].
